title: Russia Seized Nestlé's Russian Business. The New Manager Is a Ministry of Interior General.
subtitle: Western and exile press surfaced the insider-enrichment mechanics; Russian state press reported it as routine
body_md:
Vladimir Putin signed a decree on September 17 placing Russian subsidiaries of Nestlé, Auchan, and Leroy Merlin under temporary management by a company called L.E.V. Management. Neither Nestlé nor Auchan had exited Russia following the 2022 invasion. The estimated value of the Nestlé assets alone is up to 1.7 billion Swiss francs, per Deutsche Welle Deutsch. Nestlé shares fell 1.5% in Zurich on news of the decree.

The fact that attracted the most attention in Western and exile coverage was not the seizure itself but the entity receiving control. [Meduza](https://meduza.io/en/news/2026/09/17/putin-put-russian-assets-of-french-supermarket-chain-auchan-and-swiss-food-giant-nestle-under-temporary-management-neither-company-had-left-russia-after-the-full-scale-invasion) identified L.E.V. Management's general director as Andrei Krayushkin — an Interior Ministry major general and former first deputy head of the migration department. Meduza was the only outlet to name and contextualise the security-service identity of the new controlling entity. A company registered in late 2025 and run by a serving Interior Ministry general is now managing assets worth over a billion euros that belong to one of the world's largest food companies.

[AFP / France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260918-russia-seizes-assets-of-swiss-food-giant-nestle-and-three-french-firms) framed the move within the pattern: "Most Western companies quickly sold their Russian operations and holdings after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the Kremlin has since made it difficult for firms to leave the country." Both Nestlé and Auchan chose to stay. The decree is what that choice eventually produced.

[Moscow Times](https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2026/09/18/nestle-weighing-all-options-after-kremlin-takes-control-of-its-russian-business-a93745) was the clearest on the political economy underneath the legal action: "Moscow has also used the law to raise cash through forced sales, exit taxes and discounts, while rewarding Kremlin-loyal insiders." The Danone precedent makes this concrete. [Standard Kenya World](https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/world/article/2001558103/russia-seizes-assets-of-nestle-french-firms) provided the clearest telling of that precedent: Moscow's 2023 takeover of Danone's Russian business "was later sold to a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov." The legal mechanism of temporary administration has historically been a waypoint on the path to insider acquisition, not a permanent state.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov offered the public justification to [Argumenty i Fakty](https://aif.ru/politics/peskov-obyasnil-reshenie-peredat-aktivy-ashana-i-nestle) — a Russian state-aligned outlet — stating that the assets were being transferred because the companies belong to nations "actively involved in hostilities against Russia." The Peskov quote is reported in Russian state press as a self-sufficient explanation, with no further context about asset value, employee impact, legal mechanism, or precedent. Western and exile outlets treat it as a framing device for what is functionally a seizure.

Nestlé's response to Meduza's coverage was: "Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees." Auchan informed Kommersant it had requested "clarifications." Both responses are notable for what they do not claim: neither denies the decree's validity or announces immediate legal challenge.

One country is conspicuously absent from this 13-outlet corpus: Switzerland. Nestlé is headquartered in Vevey; the Swiss investor-rights and corporate-governance angle on the seizure — the domestic story for the company's home country — does not appear. The financial dimension (Swiss institutional investors, the SIX listing, Swiss media business press) and the political dimension (Swiss neutrality policy in relation to Russian sanctions) both remain unreported. The story of what Russia has done to Switzerland's most valuable food company is, in Swiss media terms, not yet in this corpus.
